description: Digital giants often pay derisory taxes compared to their profits. This is not always illegal: it is the result of loopholes in international law.

hero.hook: In 2014, Apple paid an effective tax rate of close to 0.005% in Ireland. How is this possible?

blocks.text: GAFAM, that is to say Google, Apple, Facebook (Meta), Amazon and Microsoft, are among the richest companies in the world. However, in proportion to their profits, they often pay much less tax than a traditional SME.

This is not fraud in the strict sense: it is **tax optimization**, that is to say the skillful exploitation of loopholes in international law. This mechanism deprives States of hundreds of billions of dollars each year. Here's how it works, and how the world is trying to respond to it.

The international tax system was designed at the beginning of the 20th century for an industrial economy: a company had to own factories or offices in a country, what is called a , to be taxed there. [[permanent establishment]]

Digital technology has broken this link with the territory. Today, a company can dominate a market, capture the data of millions of users and make a lot of money in a country, without owning a single building there. She can then separate the place where she earns her money from the place where she declares it.
In 2014, the U.S. IRS found that Microsoft had shifted $39 billion in profits to Puerto Rico through intellectual property rights, saving more than $6.5 billion in taxes.

sections.title: A tax designed for factories, not for digital

blocks.text: According to the OECD, these practices cost public budgets around the world between $100 and $240 billion per year, or 4 to 10% of all corporate taxes collected on the planet.

blocks.caption: The European headquarters of digital giants are often located in countries where taxes are lowest.

blocks.text: This shortfall forces states to choose between increasing taxes on households and SMEs, or reducing public spending such as health or education. A local company pays a much higher tax rate on average than a multinational, which creates unfair competition.

sections.title: A shortfall of hundreds of billions

blocks.text: In 2021, under the aegis of the OECD and the G20, a historic agreement established a . It targets companies whose turnover exceeds 750 million euros: if they only pay 5% taxes in a country, their country of origin can now claim the missing 10%. [[global minimum tax of 15%]]

Some countries, such as France, have also created a national tax directly targeting the turnover of digital giants. At the same time, multinationals must now publish, country by country, the location of their employees, their profits and their taxes: transparency which makes it possible to identify the most glaring discrepancies.

sections.title: The response: a global minimum tax

blocks.text: Ireland, with its official tax rate of 12.5% ​​and its secret agreements called , has become the European pivot of tax optimization. Thanks to a complex structure, Apple paid an effective tax rate close to 0.005% in 2014. [[tax rulings]]

The European Commission has demanded 13 billion euros in unpaid taxes from Apple from Ireland, but the country has long refused to collect them: it fears that too strict rules will cause head offices to flee to other regions of the world. Defenders of tax justice also point out that this rate of 15% remains lower than the average for developed countries, and that the poorest countries, often those most affected by tax evasion, will only recover a tiny share.

GAFAM have long taken advantage of loopholes in international law to pay derisory taxes, costing public budgets up to $240 billion per year. Since 2021, a global minimum tax of 15% has attempted to correct this imbalance, but the battle for fairer taxation continues.

title: Tax evasion by multinationals
